items.title: L14: LET: naming parts of a formula
items.body:
LET lets you give names to values or calculations inside a single formula, then use those names. The syntax is LET(name1, value1, name2, value2, ..., calculation). The last argument is always the calculation that produces the result. Suppose B2:B6 holds 12, 18, 9, 21 and 15. The formula =LET(t,SUM(B2:B6),n,COUNT(B2:B6),t/n) defines t as the total, 75, and n as the count, 5, and returns 75/5 = 15.

The benefits are practical. A long formula that repeats the same sub-calculation, for example SUM(B2:B6) three times, can name it once. The formula is shorter, easier to read and quicker to audit. In large files it can also calculate faster, because the repeated part is evaluated once.

Names exist only inside the formula. They cannot be used in other cells, and they are not workbook names. A name must start with a letter, cannot look like a cell reference such as A1 or R1C1, and must not contain spaces. Each name can use the names defined before it. In =LET(a,5,b,a*2,b+1), b is 10 and the result is 11. A name cannot refer to one defined after it.

LET is available in current Microsoft 365 and recent Excel versions. A workbook opened in an older version shows #NAME? where LET is used, so check what the users have before relying on it. LET works well with dynamic array functions; for example, a filtered list can be held in a name and then counted and summed from the same name.

LAMBDA goes a step further and lets you define your own reusable function, but this needs careful documentation. Name, test and describe anything that other people will rely on. Do not use LET to make a formula more clever than the team can maintain.

items.title: L14: Multi-criteria totals and averages with dates
items.source: Microsoft Support: SUMPRODUCT, SUMIFS and AVERAGEIFS functions
items.body:
Consider six invoices. Ops: 10 January £400; Ops: 15 February £250; HR: 20 February £300; Ops: 5 March £150; HR: 25 March £500; HR: 30 March £100. The dates are in column B, departments in column A and amounts in column C.

A manager asks for spending between 1 February and 31 March. The qualifying invoices are all those from 15 February onwards, so the total is 250 + 300 + 150 + 500 + 100 = £1,300. Of that, Ops accounts for 250 + 150 = £400, which is 400/1,300 = 30.8%, and HR for £900. The formula =SUMIFS(C:C,A:A,"Ops",B:B,">="&DATE(2025,2,1),B:B,"<"&DATE(2025,4,1)) returns 400. Using "<"&DATE(2025,4,1) rather than "<=31 March" protects against dates that carry a time.

An average needs a matching count. Ops across the whole period has three invoices totalling £800, so the average invoice is £266.67. =AVERAGEIFS(C:C,A:A,"Ops") gives it directly. Note that AVERAGEIFS returns #DIV/0! if no rows meet the criteria, whereas SUMIFS returns 0. The equivalent with SUMPRODUCT is =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A7="Ops")*C2:C7)/SUMPRODUCT(--(A2:A7="Ops")).

A weighted average is not the average of averages. If Ops averages £266.67 on three invoices and HR averages £300 on three invoices, the overall average is £283.33, which happens to equal the simple mean here only because the counts are equal. With unequal counts, the larger group counts for more. Always compute total divided by total.

Check by reconciling: the department totals should add to the overall total, and the sum of the monthly totals should equal the whole. A mismatch usually means a boundary has been missed or counted twice, such as a date at the end of a month.

items.title: L14: Budget profiles, variance and forecast outturn
items.source: HM Treasury: Managing Public Money; departmental financial management guidance
items.body:
A manager is responsible for a budget and must explain how it is going. Take an annual budget of £120,000 phased evenly, so £10,000 a month. After four months the profiled budget is £40,000. Actual spend to date is £46,000. Variance is usually actual minus budget, so +£6,000 means an overspend. As a percentage of the year-to-date budget it is 6,000/40,000 = 15%. State the sign convention, because some reports show underspends as positive.

A simple forecast of outturn, the expected year-end position, extends the run rate: 46,000 / 4 months x 12 months = £138,000, which is £18,000 over budget. That assumes spending continues at the same rate. It is a starting point, not a conclusion, because spending is often lumpy.

Suppose £12,000 of the spend was a one-off item. The underlying run rate is (46,000 - 12,000) / 4 x 12 = £102,000 a year. Adding the one-off back gives a forecast outturn of £114,000, which is £6,000 under budget. The same figures lead to opposite messages, so identify one-off and timing items before you forecast.

Phasing matters. A budget phased evenly does not suit a cost that falls in one quarter, such as an annual licence. Profile the budget in line with expected timing, so that variances reflect real overspending, not timing.

Spend is recorded when the cost is incurred, not when the invoice is paid. Goods received but not yet invoiced should be accrued. Check the accounting period, otherwise a cost may fall in the wrong month.

A typical tolerance for reporting is plus or minus a few per cent, often with a RAG status. Report the variance, the reason, the forecast and the action. Do not hide an overspend: raise it early with finance and your line manager.

items.title: L14: Reconciling a pivot to its source
items.source: Government Analysis Function: Quality guidance; Microsoft Support: PivotTable data
items.body:
A pivot table that does not agree with its source is a common and embarrassing error. Suppose the source of 1,000 rows totals £250,000, but the pivot grand total is £248,500. The difference is £1,500. A systematic approach finds the cause.

Start with the basics. Is the pivot refreshed? Does the source range cover all rows, or has it stopped short? Are any report filters, slicers or row-label filters hiding items? Does the pivot show a "(blank)" item, which means a blank in the row field and tells you that some records have no department?

Next, check how the amounts are stored. A pivot set to Sum treats numbers stored as text as zero, so these rows add nothing. If three rows of £500 are stored as text, the pivot is short by £1,500, which would explain the gap here. Find them with =SUMPRODUCT(--ISTEXT(C2:C1001)) or by checking the cells' alignment. Convert them to numbers, refresh and compare again. Note that a pivot field containing any text will tend to default to Count. If the field shows Count of Amount, change it to Sum.

Then look at logic. A calculated field is the sum of its parts, so a ratio field gives total divided by total, not the average of row ratios. Hidden rows in the source still count in a pivot.

Document what you found and fix it in the source, not in the pivot. Record the reconciliation as a short table: source total, pivot total, difference, cause, and the corrected figure. Include the check cell on the report page so that a future reader can see it agrees.

items.title: L14: Sensitivity and scenarios: testing a cost model
items.source: HM Treasury: The Green Book and Aqua Book guidance on uncertainty and sensitivity
items.body:
A cost model multiplies a volume by a unit cost. In the base case, 2,000 units at £45 each give £90,000. Decision-makers want to know how sure that figure is. Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time to see its effect. A 10% rise in volume gives 2,200 x £45 = £99,000. A 5% rise in unit cost gives 2,000 x £47.25 = £94,500. Together they give 2,200 x £47.25 = £103,950, a rise of 15.5%, slightly more than the 15% you get by adding 10% and 5%. When inputs multiply, effects combine multiplicatively.

Scenario analysis changes several inputs at once to describe a coherent situation, such as a low, central and high case. Label the scenarios and state what each assumes. A range is more honest than a single point. Put all inputs in separate cells so that the scenarios can be switched, for example with a selector cell and CHOOSE or INDEX.

Goal Seek works backwards. To find the volume that gives a cost of £100,000 at £45 a unit, divide 100,000 by 45, which is 2,222.2. Because volume is a whole number, 2,222 units cost £99,990 and 2,223 cost £100,035. Think about rounding direction: a cap on spend is breached by 2,223. Goal Seek changes a cell and leaves the result there, so record what it was before.

A one-way data table can show results across a range of inputs without copying formulas. 

Show what drives the answer. A tornado chart or a ranked table of impacts shows which inputs matter most. Spend effort on checking those inputs. State the main assumptions on the page, with their source. An unlabelled central case invites the question "how did you get that?"

items.title: L14: Rolling windows and moving averages
items.source: Microsoft Support: EDATE, EOMONTH and AVERAGE functions; ONS: guidance on time series
items.body:
Reports often need a rolling 12 months, which moves forward each month, so that the latest figure always covers a full year. To total the 12 months to a month end in cell E1, such as 31 March 2025, the lower limit is the end of the same month a year earlier, 31 March 2024, used with "greater than". The formula is =SUMIFS(Amt,Date,">"&EOMONTH(E1,-12),Date,"<="&E1). It covers 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025, which is 12 months. A common slip is to use ">="&EDATE(E1,-12), which gives 31 March 2024 and includes one day too many from the previous year.

EOMONTH is the better choice for month-end reporting, because EDATE keeps the same day number and can behave inconsistently across months of different lengths. 

A moving average smooths short-term ups and downs. Suppose four months show 100, 120, 90 and 110. The three-month moving average for March is (100 + 120 + 90)/3 = 103.33. For April it is (120 + 90 + 110)/3 = 106.67. The first two months have no value, because there are not enough previous points. Write the formula so that it only appears when a full window exists, and do not fill the early cells with zeros, which would drag the line down.

A moving average lags the data. It reacts late to a turning point and the lag grows with the window. A rolling total of 12 months removes seasonality, which is why it is useful for annual comparisons.

Do not compare a rolling figure with a single month. Compare like with like: 12 months against 12 months, or one month against the same month last year. State the period in the title and say if the latest month is provisional.

items.title: L14: What clearance changes in a submission: finance, legal and equalities
items.source: HM Treasury: Managing Public Money; Equality Act 2010, section 149; Cabinet Office guidance on submissions
items.body:
Before a submission reaches a minister, specialists check it. A manager should know what each is checking and when to ask.

Finance checks affordability and value for money. Is the spend within the budget and delegated limits? Are the costs and assumptions sound? Does the proposal need Treasury approval? Spending above a department's delegated authority needs Treasury consent, so involve finance early. The accounting officer, usually the permanent secretary, has personal responsibility for propriety, regularity, value for money and feasibility. If a minister proposes something the accounting officer judges to breach one of these tests, the accounting officer can ask for a written ministerial direction.

Legal advice covers whether the department has the power to act (often called vires), the risk of legal challenge, and procedural duties, such as consultation. Legal advice is privileged. Do not quote it in documents that may be disclosed or shared outside government unless lawyers agree, and mark legally privileged documents.

The public sector equality duty requires due regard to the effect of decisions on people with protected characteristics. An equality analysis should be done before the decision, not after, and be based on evidence. It shows how the minister has considered the impact, and it must be real, not a form filled in later.

Devolved administrations or other departments may need to see the paper where their interests are affected, and a submission should say what consultation has taken place. Clearances take time, so plan them into the timetable and record who cleared what and when.

Never state that a paper has been cleared when it has not. If advisers disagree, say so and set out the difference.

items.title: L14: Correcting an error in advice, figures or statements
items.source: Ministerial Code; Civil Service Code; UK Statistics Authority: Code of Practice for Statistics
items.body:
Errors happen. What matters is how quickly and openly they are corrected. The Civil Service Code requires honesty and integrity: officials must not deceive or knowingly mislead ministers, Parliament or the public. If you discover that a figure or fact you provided was wrong, tell your line manager at once, and tell those who have relied on it. Do not wait to see if anyone notices.

If a minister has used the wrong information in Parliament, the Ministerial Code says ministers who have inadvertently misled Parliament must correct the record at the earliest opportunity. The private office, with the relevant policy team, will arrange for a correction to be made, for example through a written statement or a letter to the relevant committee. Your job is to provide the right facts, an explanation of what went wrong and the effect, quickly.

For published statistics, the Code of Practice for Statistics requires that errors are corrected promptly and transparently. The correction is published with a clear explanation of what changed and why, and users are told. Quietly replacing a file does not meet this standard. Keep a revisions log, and notify anyone who may have used the earlier numbers.

When you find an error, do these things: establish the facts, assess the effect (who has seen it and what decisions might have depended on it), correct the source, tell those affected, and find the cause so that it does not recur. Record the incident and the action.

A culture that blames individuals hides errors. Managers should make it safe to report problems early, while expecting people to check their work. Learn from near misses as well as actual errors. Where the error involves personal data, the breach process may also apply.

Wait for further instructions from the minister

questions.hint: The impact assessment shapes the response.

questions.prompt: Why does blaming individuals make errors worse?

options.text: It speeds up the correction of errors
It improves the quality of checking
People hide mistakes rather than reporting them
It reduces the number of errors made

questions.hint: Safe reporting leads to earlier fixes.

questions.prompt: What is the value of recording near misses?

options.text: It increases the workload without any benefit
It allows staff to be disciplined for slips
It shows that checking is not needed
It shows weaknesses before they cause real errors

questions.hint: Learning from near misses prevents future errors.

questions.prompt: An error involves personal data being sent to the wrong person. Which other process applies?

options.text: The personal data breach process
The FOI process
The ministerial direction process
The parliamentary question process

questions.hint: Breach reporting rules may apply too.

items.title: L14: Consultation principles and the duty to consider responses
items.source: Cabinet Office: Consultation principles; R v Brent LBC ex parte Gunning (the Gunning principles)
items.body:
Government consultation asks the public or groups for views before a decision. The Cabinet Office Consultation Principles (2018) set the expectation that consultations are proportionate, accessible, clear and open to those affected. They no longer set a default 12 week period: the length should suit the proposal and the people affected, and departments should justify a short consultation. The longer period may be right for complex or contentious proposals, or for consultations covering holiday periods.

The courts have set four legal tests, known as the Gunning principles. First, consultation must happen when proposals are still at a formative stage, so a decision must not already have been made. Second, the consultation must give sufficient reasons and information so that people can respond intelligently. Third, adequate time must be given for consideration and response. Fourth, the product of consultation must be conscientiously taken into account when the decision is made. Breaching any of these can mean a court overturning the decision.

Practical points follow. Ask clear questions, in plain English, and say what is fixed and what is open. Be careful about leading questions. Record every response, and analyse them carefully, not only counting those in favour. Respondents' personal data must be handled under the UK GDPR: say in the consultation how data will be used and published, and that responses may be disclosed under FOI.

After the consultation, publish a response that explains what was heard, how it influenced the decision, and the reasons for any changes or for not changing. Keep the evidence trail. Officials advising ministers must present the responses accurately, including the unwelcome ones, so that the minister can take them into account conscientiously.

questions.prompt: What do the Consultation Principles say about the length of consultations?

options.text: It should be proportionate, with no default 12 week period
It must be exactly 12 weeks in every case
It must be at least six months for major changes
It need not be stated in the consultation document

questions.prompt: At what stage must a consultation begin to satisfy the first Gunning test?

options.text: Once the final decision has been drafted
While proposals are still at a formative stage
After the minister has announced the preferred option
When the impact assessment has been published

questions.hint: A decision must not already have been made.

questions.prompt: A consultation paper gives only a one-line summary of the proposal. Which Gunning test does it risk failing?

options.text: Sufficient reasons and information to respond intelligently
Adequate time for consideration and response
Conscientious consideration of the product of consultation
Consultation while proposals are at a formative stage

questions.hint: People cannot respond sensibly without enough information.

questions.prompt: What does the fourth Gunning test require once responses have been received?

options.text: That they are conscientiously taken into account in the decision
That the decision follows the view of the majority of respondents
That every respondent is answered individually in writing
That the results are sent to the press before the decision

questions.hint: Responses must be weighed, not necessarily followed.

questions.prompt: A department consults but has already decided. Which principle is breached?

options.text: Adequate time must be given
The proposals must be at a formative stage
Sufficient reasons must be given
The product must be conscientiously considered

questions.prompt: What should a consultation make clear about its questions?

options.text: What is fixed and what is open to change
Which answers the department would prefer to receive
How long each answer should be
Which groups are unlikely to be heard

questions.hint: People need to know what they can influence.

questions.prompt: Why are leading questions a risk?

options.text: They can undermine the fairness of the consultation
They are harder to analyse afterwards
They make responses longer than needed
They cost more to publish in accessible formats

questions.prompt: What should the consultation say about respondents' data?

options.text: That it will not be shared under any circumstances
That it is exempt from the UK GDPR as consultation data
How it will be used and published, and that it may be disclosed under FOI
Nothing, since responses to consultations are public

questions.prompt: What should the published consultation response include?

options.text: Only the number of respondents in favour
What was heard, how it influenced the decision and why
The names and addresses of all respondents
Only the department's original proposal

questions.hint: It shows how responses were taken into account.

questions.prompt: What must officials do when presenting responses to a minister?

options.text: Present only the responses that support the proposal
Summarise them all in one line
Present them accurately, including the unwelcome ones
Leave out responses from campaign groups

questions.hint: Conscientious consideration needs an honest picture.

items.title: L14: Lawful basis in awkward cases: staff, children and changed purposes
items.source: ICO: Guide to the UK GDPR, lawful basis, children and purpose limitation
items.body:
Lawful basis choices become harder in real cases. Consider the common examples.

Staff data. Consent is a poor basis for processing employee data because of the imbalance of power: an employee may feel unable to refuse. Employers usually rely on contract (to pay staff and manage employment), legal obligation (tax and right to work checks) and, for public bodies, public task. Health data about staff also needs an Article 9 condition, often employment law.

Children. Children's data deserves particular care. If consent is the basis for online services offered directly to a child, the UK sets the age at 13 below which parental consent is needed.

Consent. When used, consent must be a clear, affirmative, specific and informed choice; silence or pre-ticked boxes do not count. It must be as easy to withdraw as to give, and withdrawal must be actioned. Do not treat consent as a back-up basis: if you ask for consent and then cannot honour a refusal, you have misled the person. If consent is not the real basis, do not ask for it.

Vital interests applies only to matters of life and death where the person cannot give consent.

Changing purpose. Data collected for one purpose cannot be reused for an incompatible one. Test compatibility by looking at the link between purposes, the context and reasonable expectations, the nature of the data, the consequences, and safeguards. Use for a new purpose usually needs a new lawful basis or fresh consent unless it is compatible, or the new use is required by law. Always tell people through a privacy notice.

Record the decision, the reasoning and the person who made it.

questions.prompt: Why is consent usually a poor basis for processing employee data?

options.text: Employee data is exempt from the UK GDPR
There is an imbalance of power, so consent may not be free
Employers are not allowed to hold health data
Consent cannot be recorded for staff

questions.prompt: Which basis would an employer typically use to pay staff?

options.text: Contract
Vital interests
Consent
Legitimate interests only

questions.hint: Pay is part of the employment contract.

questions.prompt: Below what age is parental consent needed for online services offered directly to a child, where consent is the basis?
Which is a valid consent under the UK GDPR?

options.text: A clear affirmative action by an informed person
A pre-ticked box on a form
Silence after a notice has been sent
Continued use of the service after a change

questions.hint: Consent must be an affirmative choice.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with asking for consent as a back-up when another basis really applies?

options.text: It costs more to administer than other bases
It is allowed only for children's data
It breaches the Official Secrets Act
It misleads the person if you cannot honour a refusal

questions.prompt: When does the vital interests basis apply?

options.text: To any matter that is in the public interest
To business continuity planning
To life-and-death matters where the person cannot consent
To staff welfare and wellbeing schemes

questions.prompt: Data collected for casework is to be used for an unrelated marketing exercise. What is the first question?

options.text: Is it cheaper to reuse the data than to collect new data?
Is the new purpose compatible with the original?
Has the team collected enough data for the exercise?
Is the data stored in the UK?

questions.prompt: Which factor helps to test compatibility of a new purpose?

options.text: The size of the team holding the data
The cost of the system that stores it
The person's reasonable expectations
The age of the database itself

questions.hint: Expectations are part of the test.

questions.prompt: What should happen if the new purpose is incompatible?

options.text: Nothing, because the data is already held
The ICO decides whether the use may proceed
The data subject is charged for the new use
A new lawful basis or fresh consent is usually needed

questions.prompt: What should be recorded about a lawful basis decision?

options.text: The decision, the reasoning and who made it
Only the decision reached
Only the name of the team responsible
Nothing, since the choice is obvious

items.title: L14: Sending personal data abroad: transfers and cloud tools
items.source: ICO: International transfers; UK GDPR Chapter V; Data Protection Act 2018
items.body:
Personal data can only be sent outside the UK, known as a restricted transfer, if there is a lawful route. Access from abroad also counts: a supplier's support staff viewing UK data from another country can amount to a transfer.

The usual routes in the UK GDPR are, in order of preference. First, adequacy regulations, where the UK government has decided that a country or territory provides an essentially equivalent level of protection. If an adequacy decision covers the destination, data can flow without further safeguards. Second, appropriate safeguards, such as the International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA), or the UK Addendum to the EU's standard contractual clauses. Where these are used, the exporter should carry out a transfer risk assessment, considering whether the destination's laws and practices could undermine the protection. Third, in limited cases, exceptions such as explicit consent or necessity for important reasons of public interest. The exceptions are for occasional and specific cases, not routine transfers.

A manager buying or using a service should ask where the data is stored and processed, where support staff are based, who the sub-processors are, and whether data can be accessed from other countries. Contracts should include the processor terms required by Article 28 and cover transfers.

For government data, security classification also matters. Some material cannot go overseas at all, regardless of data protection routes, and a security assessment may be needed. Hosting UK government data abroad needs specific approval and advice from security and data protection teams.

A DPIA should record the transfers. Tell people in your privacy notice that their data may be transferred and on what basis.

questions.prompt: What is a restricted transfer?

options.text: Sending data between two UK departments
Sending data by post rather than electronically
Sending personal data to a recipient outside the UK
Sending data to a different building

questions.hint: The term concerns transfers across the UK border.

questions.prompt: A supplier's support team in another country can view UK personal data. What does this amount to?

options.text: Nothing, as the data stays on the UK server
A breach in every case
An FOI disclosure
A transfer that needs a lawful route

questions.hint: Remote access can count as a transfer.

questions.prompt: What does an adequacy decision mean?

options.text: The destination has signed up to the IDTA
The data is encrypted while it is in transit
The data subject has agreed to the transfer
The destination's protection is judged essentially equivalent, so no further safeguard is needed

questions.prompt: Which is an appropriate safeguard where there is no adequacy?

options.text: A verbal assurance from the supplier
The International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA)
A press statement from the receiving organisation
A signed FOI request from the supplier

questions.hint: It is a standard contract for transfers.

questions.prompt: What should the exporter assess when relying on the IDTA?

options.text: The price of the service being bought
The size of the data file being sent
The staffing levels of the supplier
Whether the destination's laws could undermine the protection

questions.hint: This is a transfer risk assessment.

questions.prompt: What are the exceptions such as explicit consent suited to?

options.text: All routine cloud services
Regular large transfers to one supplier
Occasional and specific transfers, not routine ones
Transfers by processors only

questions.prompt: Before approving a cloud tool, which question is most relevant?

options.text: Does the tool have a recognisable brand?
How many other organisations use the tool?
Where is the data stored and who can access it from where?
Is the tool free to try for a month?

questions.hint: Location and access decide the transfer position.

questions.prompt: Why might some government material be barred from overseas hosting whatever the data protection route?

options.text: Security classification can restrict where it may be held
Because the UK GDPR forbids all transfers
Because encryption is not allowed outside the UK
Because overseas suppliers cannot sign contracts

questions.prompt: Where should transfers be recorded and explained?

options.text: In the press office log
In the DPIA and the privacy notice
In the minutes of the board
In the supplier's marketing material

questions.hint: Transparency and risk assessment both need to cover it.

questions.prompt: Which contract term is required where a processor handles the data?

options.text: A non-compete clause
A clause on use of the supplier's branding
The Article 28 processor terms
A clause on the supplier's staff holidays

items.title: L14: Official business in chat apps and the corporate record
items.source: Cabinet Office: Guidance on use of non-corporate communication channels; The National Archives: Records management
items.body:
Messaging apps and chat tools are convenient, and decisions are often made in them. If the discussion relates to official business, the content is official information and may be a record. It can be requested under the Freedom of Information Act or a subject access request, and it may be needed for a public inquiry or litigation. The medium does not change that.

Government guidance says that official business should be conducted on corporate systems wherever possible. Non-corporate channels, such as personal text messaging or WhatsApp on a personal phone, should be used only if there is no practical alternative, and any substantive business, such as a decision or an instruction, should be moved to the corporate record as soon as possible. Do not rely on disappearing messages: turning them on may mean the record is lost, and deliberate deletion to avoid disclosure is an offence under section 77 of the Freedom of Information Act.

Corporate chat tools, such as those inside the department's collaboration platform, are subject to a retention setting. Find out how long messages are kept, and do not assume chats are permanent. If a chat contains a decision, copy it to the file. Keep chat for the quick questions it suits, and use email or a document for formal instructions, advice and approvals.

Group chats raise special risks. Messages can be forwarded or screenshotted, members can join and leave, and sensitive material can end up with people who should not have it. Classification still applies: do not put OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE material into a channel not approved for it.

A manager sets the tone: agree team rules on what goes in chat and what is recorded, and make them explicit.

questions.prompt: What is the status of a chat message that records an official decision?

options.text: It is private because of the medium used
It is official information and may be a record
It is exempt from the Freedom of Information Act
It is automatically deleted after 24 hours

questions.hint: The medium does not change the nature of the content.

questions.prompt: Where should official business be conducted?

options.text: On personal phones, if staff prefer
On corporate systems wherever possible
On any app the team finds convenient
In disappearing message groups

questions.prompt: A decision is taken on a personal messaging app because no alternative was available. What should happen?

options.text: Leave it in the app, which already counts as the record
Delete it to protect the people involved
Move it to the corporate record as soon as possible
Wait until an FOI request arrives

questions.prompt: Why is relying on disappearing messages risky?

options.text: Records may be lost, and deliberate deletion to avoid disclosure is an offence
They use too much storage on the device
They are not supported on all phones
They do not allow attachments to be sent

questions.hint: Section 77 covers destruction to prevent disclosure.

questions.prompt: What should a manager check about the department's chat tool?

options.text: Which emojis the tool supports
Which colour themes the tool offers
How long messages are retained
How many users may join a channel

questions.prompt: Which communication suits a formal instruction?

options.text: Email or a document, kept on the file
A group chat with the team
A voice note on a messaging app
A direct message to the individual

questions.hint: Formal advice and approvals need a durable record.

questions.prompt: What is a particular risk of group chats?

options.text: They are always encrypted end to end
Messages can be forwarded, and sensitive material can reach the wrong people
They cannot be searched by the department
They are limited to ten members at a time

questions.hint: Control over the audience is weak.

questions.prompt: Does classification still apply in a chat channel?

options.text: It does not, if the chat is informal
It does, so OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE material must not go in an unapproved channel
It applies only to emails sent outside the department
It applies only to attachments, not messages

questions.hint: Handling rules apply to the information.

questions.prompt: What is the manager's role in setting team practice?

options.text: Ban all use of chat tools in the team
Agree explicit rules on what goes in chat and what is recorded
Leave each member of staff to decide
Review every chat personally each week

items.title: L14: Governing an AI tool: assessment, bias and transparency
items.source: UK Government: Generative AI Framework for HMG; Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard; ICO: AI and data protection guidance
items.body:
When a team wants to use an AI tool in a service, not just for personal drafting, there are more questions to ask. A manager should expect these steps.

Define the purpose and the decision. What is the tool for? Does it inform a human decision, or make one? Where it could affect people's rights or services, it needs a higher level of care. The UK GDPR restricts decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects. If a tool is used, a person must be able to review, challenge and change the outcome, and the review must be real.

Do a DPIA. A new AI use that involves personal data is likely to be high risk. It should consider the data used to train and operate the tool, how it is secured, where it is processed, whether the supplier can use the data for its own purposes, and what the supplier's contract says about retention and sub-processors.

Test for accuracy and bias. Check the tool on realistic data and for different groups. A tool can perform well on average but poorly for some groups. Agree measures of success before testing. Test again after changes, since performance can drift.

Be able to explain. People should be told when AI is used and be able to understand, in plain terms, how a decision was reached. A tool that cannot be explained is hard to defend if challenged. Publish information about the tool: government has a recording standard for algorithmic transparency, which public bodies are encouraged to use for tools that affect decisions about people.

Set accountability. Name an owner, plan monitoring, and decide when to stop using it.

Never treat approval of a tool for one use as approval for all uses.

questions.prompt: Which question matters most when assessing an AI tool in a service?

options.text: Does it inform a human decision, or make one?
How modern does the interface look?
How many languages does the supplier support?
How long has the supplier been trading?

questions.hint: Solely automated significant decisions are restricted.

questions.prompt: What does the UK GDPR require when decisions with significant effects use an AI tool?

options.text: The tool must make all of the final decisions
Each decision must be sent to the ICO for approval
A person must be able to review, challenge and change the outcome
The tool must be built in-house

questions.prompt: Why is a DPIA likely for a new AI use involving personal data?

options.text: It is cheaper than the alternative
The ICO asks for one for every project
The tool is unlawful by default
It is likely to present a high risk to individuals

questions.hint: New technology and personal data signal high risk.

questions.prompt: Which supplier question belongs in the DPIA?

options.text: How many staff does the supplier employ?
Can the supplier use the data for its own purposes?
Which other departments have bought from the supplier?
Does the supplier offer volume discounts?

questions.hint: Supplier reuse of data changes the risk.

questions.prompt: Why test an AI tool on different groups of people?

options.text: Different groups have different budgets
It makes the testing quicker to complete
It may perform well on average but poorly for some groups
Groups must be tested separately by law

questions.prompt: Why should success measures be agreed before testing?

options.text: It shortens the time the testing takes
It avoids the need for a DPIA
It satisfies the supplier's contract
So the results cannot be bent to suit the outcome

questions.prompt: Why re-test after changes?

options.text: Testing is cheaper after changes are made
The supplier requires it under the contract
The ICO checks the results each time
Performance can drift when the tool or data changes

questions.prompt: What is the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard for?

options.text: Recording staff hours spent on automation
Certifying software for security
Publishing information about algorithmic tools used in decisions
Setting maximum prices for AI tools

questions.prompt: What does naming an owner and planning monitoring achieve?

options.text: A lower cost for running the tool
Clear accountability for performance, complaints and when to stop
Less need for a contract with the supplier
A faster procurement process

questions.prompt: A tool is approved for drafting internal notes. Can it then be used to score customers' claims?

options.text: It can, as the tool itself is now approved for all uses
It can, if the team agrees in a meeting
Not automatically, because approval for one use does not cover another
It can, if it proves cheaper than the current method

questions.hint: Each use needs its own assessment.
